SEARCH
Package com.falkordb

Interface GraphContext.Transaction

All Superinterfaces:
AutoCloseable, Closeable
Enclosing interface:
GraphContext
public static interface GraphContext.Transaction extends Closeable
A transaction on a GraphContext's connection: MULTI is sent when it starts, the commands are queued on the server, and exec() runs them all at once. Each command returns a Reply, which can be read once exec() ran the transaction. Get one with GraphContext.transaction(), after GraphContext.watch(String...) if the transaction must not run once a key has changed: 

 try (GraphContext context = graph.getContext()) {
     context.watch("social");
     GraphContext.Transaction transaction = context.transaction();
     Reply<ResultSet> created = transaction.query("CREATE (:Person {name: 'Alice'})");
     transaction.sendCommand("INCR", "people");
     if (transaction.exec() == null) {
         // aborted: another client changed the graph since watch(); nothing ran
     } else {
         System.out.println(created.get().getStatistics().nodesCreated());
     }
 }

FalkorDB itself has no transactions: this is the MULTI/EXEC of Redis (or Valkey) applied to graph commands, not a database transaction.

  • The queued commands run back to back at EXEC, with no other client's command in between.
  • Nothing is rolled back. If a queued command fails while it runs, such as a graph query the server rejects, the commands before it stay applied and the ones after it still run; the failure is that command's element of the list exec() returns, and what its Reply throws. Only a command the server rejects while it is queued, such as one with the wrong number of arguments, aborts the whole transaction (EXECABORT), and then nothing runs.
  • Replies arrive only at EXEC, so a decision can't be made inside the transaction on what it read. For optimistic concurrency, watch the keys first: EXEC then runs nothing, and returns null, if one of them changed.
  • In a Redis Cluster every key the transaction touches must be in the same hash slot as the graph's: give them the graph's name as a hash tag.
  • For changes to a graph that must apply all together or not at all, put them in one Cypher query.

A transaction is used once: after exec() or discard() nothing can be queued on it. The replies are decoded by exec(), as for the deprecated GraphTransaction, which describes how a deleteGraph() affects the replies queued before it. A reply that fails to decode throws the same exception on every Reply.get(). As in the rest of the client's API, the server's error replies are GraphExceptions, and a connection that can't be opened, or fails, throws a FalkorDBConnectionException. COPY of the graph can't be queued in a transaction: FalkorDB doesn't support it there.

Until the transaction ends, the context's connection is its own: the context runs none of its own commands, watch included, and no other pipeline or transaction can be started or used on it, since what they sent would be queued inside this transaction's MULTI. Each throws an IllegalStateException instead, as does queuing a command once the context is closed.

Like its context, a transaction is meant for one thread. Closing the context discards a transaction still open.

    • query

      Reply<ResultSet> query(String query, long timeout)
      Queues a Cypher query with a timeout.

      The timeout is sent with the query and limits how long the server runs it; 0 sets none, so the server's default (TIMEOUT_DEFAULT) applies. It doesn't change how long the client waits for the replies in exec(), which a socket (read) timeout on the connection can still end: see Graph.query(String, long).

      Parameters:
      query - Cypher query
      timeout - timeout in milliseconds; not negative
      Returns:
      the reply: the result set
      Throws:
      IllegalArgumentException - if timeout is negative; nothing is queued then

    • deleteGraph

      Reply<String> deleteGraph()
      Queues a delete of the entire graph. The client's schema cache is cleared when exec() has run the delete: not when it is queued, and not at all if the transaction is discarded or aborted. A reply queued before it is decoded with what the cache held when the delete was queued, as for GraphTransaction.deleteGraph().
      Returns:

    • sendCommand

      Reply<@Nullable Object> sendCommand(String command, String... args)
      Queues a Redis command that isn't a graph command, such as SET, GET or INCR, to run with the graph commands.

      The reply is decoded from what the server sent into JDK types: a simple or bulk string as a UTF-8 String, an integer as a Long, an array as a List of its elements decoded the same way, with a GraphException where an element is an error, and a nil reply as null. The driver speaks RESP2 unless its connection URI asks for protocol=3; then a double is a Double, a boolean a Boolean, a big number a java.math.BigInteger, a set a List and a map a LinkedHashMap, except an empty map, which is an empty List. An error reply makes reading the reply throw a GraphException.

      A command that would break this transaction, the connection or the client's schema cache is refused with an IllegalArgumentException, and nothing is sent. Command names are compared ignoring the case of ASCII letters, as Redis does:

      • commands this API runs itself: MULTI, EXEC, DISCARD, WATCH and UNWATCH (see GraphContext.transaction() and GraphContext.watch(String...)), and every GRAPH.* command, whose reply only the graph methods decode, with the client's schema cache, which they keep up to date;
      • commands that delete or replace the graph's key behind that cache, which would then decode a new graph's replies with the old graph's names: DEL, UNLINK, GETDEL, RENAME, RENAMENX, MOVE, RESTORE and MIGRATE of the graph's key, COPY to it, and FLUSHALL, FLUSHDB and SWAPDB; delete the graph with deleteGraph(). Other commands that write the graph's key aren't recognized: see below;
      • commands that change the connection's state, which outlives the context when the pool lends the connection on, or how its replies are framed: AUTH, HELLO, SELECT, CLIENT, RESET, QUIT, READONLY, READWRITE, ASKING, SCRIPT DEBUG;
      • commands that take the connection out of request and reply: SUBSCRIBE, PSUBSCRIBE, SSUBSCRIBE, UNSUBSCRIBE, PUNSUBSCRIBE, SUNSUBSCRIBE, MONITOR, SYNC, PSYNC, REPLCONF;
      • blocking commands, which hold the connection in a pipeline, so that closing the context waits for them, and don't block inside MULTI: BLPOP, BRPOP, BRPOPLPUSH, BLMOVE, BLMPOP, BZPOPMIN, BZPOPMAX, BZMPOP, WAITAOF, WAIT, DEBUG SLEEP, and XREAD or XREADGROUP with BLOCK.

      Some of these may be allowed in a later release, such as the GRAPH.* commands that don't touch a graph. Other commands are sent as they are: an overwrite of the graph's key, such as a SET of it, or its expiry, still leaves the schema cache as it was, as a change by another client would. In a cluster the context's connection is to the node that serves the graph's key, so a command on a key in another hash slot fails with a MOVED error; put the graph's name in the key as a hash tag to keep it on that node.

      Parameters:
      command - the command's name, such as "SET"
      args - its arguments
      Returns:
      the reply
      Throws:
      IllegalArgumentException - if the command is refused, command is null or empty, or args or one of its elements is null; nothing is queued then

      Reply<@Nullable Object> sendBinaryCommand(String command, byte[]... args)
      Queues a Redis command that isn't a graph command, with binary arguments, such as a SET of a binary value.

      The reply is decoded from what the server sent into JDK types: a simple or bulk string as a byte[], an integer as a Long, an array as a List of its elements decoded the same way, with a GraphException where an element is an error, and a nil reply as null. The driver speaks RESP2 unless its connection URI asks for protocol=3; then a double is a Double, a boolean a Boolean, a big number a java.math.BigInteger, a set a List and a map a LinkedHashMap (whose byte[] keys compare by identity), except an empty map, which is an empty List. An error reply makes reading the reply throw a GraphException.

      A command that would break this transaction, the connection or the client's schema cache is refused with an IllegalArgumentException, and nothing is sent. Command names are compared ignoring the case of ASCII letters, as Redis does:

      • commands this API runs itself: MULTI, EXEC, DISCARD, WATCH and UNWATCH (see GraphContext.transaction() and GraphContext.watch(String...)), and every GRAPH.* command, whose reply only the graph methods decode, with the client's schema cache, which they keep up to date;
      • commands that delete or replace the graph's key behind that cache, which would then decode a new graph's replies with the old graph's names: DEL, UNLINK, GETDEL, RENAME, RENAMENX, MOVE, RESTORE and MIGRATE of the graph's key, COPY to it, and FLUSHALL, FLUSHDB and SWAPDB; delete the graph with deleteGraph(). Other commands that write the graph's key aren't recognized: see below;
      • commands that change the connection's state, which outlives the context when the pool lends the connection on, or how its replies are framed: AUTH, HELLO, SELECT, CLIENT, RESET, QUIT, READONLY, READWRITE, ASKING, SCRIPT DEBUG;
      • commands that take the connection out of request and reply: SUBSCRIBE, PSUBSCRIBE, SSUBSCRIBE, UNSUBSCRIBE, PUNSUBSCRIBE, SUNSUBSCRIBE, MONITOR, SYNC, PSYNC, REPLCONF;
      • blocking commands, which hold the connection in a pipeline, so that closing the context waits for them, and don't block inside MULTI: BLPOP, BRPOP, BRPOPLPUSH, BLMOVE, BLMPOP, BZPOPMIN, BZPOPMAX, BZMPOP, WAITAOF, WAIT, DEBUG SLEEP, and XREAD or XREADGROUP with BLOCK.

      Some of these may be allowed in a later release, such as the GRAPH.* commands that don't touch a graph. Other commands are sent as they are: an overwrite of the graph's key, such as a SET of it, or its expiry, still leaves the schema cache as it was, as a change by another client would. In a cluster the context's connection is to the node that serves the graph's key, so a command on a key in another hash slot fails with a MOVED error; put the graph's name in the key as a hash tag to keep it on that node.

      Parameters:
      command - the command's name, such as "SET"
      args - its arguments, as bytes
      Returns:
      the reply
      Throws:
      IllegalArgumentException - if the command is refused, command is null or empty, or args or one of its elements is null; nothing is queued then

    • exec

      @Nullable List<@Nullable Object> exec()
      Runs the transaction: reads and decodes the reply to every command queued, in order. The transaction ends, and can't be used again.
      Returns:
      the decoded replies, as their Replys return them: an element is null where the reply is nil, and the exception reading the reply throws, a GraphException or the failure of a lookup decoding needed, where the command failed or its reply can't be decoded. Unmodifiable. null if the transaction was aborted, because a key the context watched changed: then no command ran, and reading a Reply of it throws an IllegalStateException saying so
      Throws:
      GraphException - if the server refused the transaction, as with EXECABORT when a command failed to queue: then no command ran
      IllegalStateException - if the transaction has ended already, the context is closed, or another pipeline or transaction on the context awaits replies

    • discard

      void discard()
      Drops the queued commands without running them, and ends the transaction; a queued deleteGraph() then leaves the schema cache alone. Keys the context watched are unwatched.
      Throws:
      IllegalStateException - if the transaction has ended already, the context is closed, or another pipeline or transaction on the context awaits replies
      GraphException - if the server rejects the DISCARD

    • close

      void close()
      Discards the transaction unless it has ended; there is nothing to do once the context is closed, which discards it. The context's connection stays open.

      Unlike Closeable.close(), this throws no checked exception.
